title: Super hacks to beat Labor’s big tax grab
full_text:
Middle-aged people are being urged to sharpen their strategies on superannuation, the last low-tax investment structure left standing amid the Albanese government’s recent tax overhaul.
When Jim Chalmers slapped minimum 30 per cent tax rates on capital gains and discretionary trusts in his May budget, superannuation’s maximum rate of 15 per cent tax during its accumulation phase and zero tax in retirement for most seniors remained untouched. That means, particularly for people in their 40s, 50s and early 60s, superannuation will become a far more attractive vehicle for building wealth and to save tax now and in the future.
While the government left superannuation taxes alone in this budget, it did strike a rushed deal with the Greens to ban borrowing for housing investment within self-managed super, and experts expect more tax tinkering in the future. Last year the government increased the tax rate for super balances above $3m, for instance. But financial specialists argue that, without knowing what the changes are, most people older than 45 are much better off focusing on building their superannuation savings.
Caveo Partners chief economist and financial strategist Theo Marinis says super rule changes are inevitable but investors need to work with what they know now. If you’re on top of other financial commitments such as debt reduction, children’s education costs or business expenses, these superannuation strategies are worth examining.
Personal contributions This year you can make up to $32,500 of tax-deductible super contributions, known as concessional contributions, although this cap includes employers’ compulsory super payments and any salary sacrifice. Nexia Sydney wealth management partner Christine Atencia says maximising these where possible will boost retirement savings while potentially reducing your tax bill.
Carry forward If you are under 75 and your super balance was below $500,000 at June 30 this year, you can make extra tax-deductible contributions using unused concessional caps from the past five financial years. “Use carry-forward concessional contributions where eligible to make larger tax-deductible contributions, particularly in years where a significant capital gain has been realised,” Atencia says.
Shift assets to super Some savvy super fund members will use the next year or two to sell some of their property, shares and other investments, then pump the money into superannuation and claim tax deductions for doing so.
Marinis says he is seeing more property investors consider this strategy ahead of a tougher tax regime from July 2027. Many landlords have ignored super while building their property portfolios and may have large carry-forward amounts available.
“If you haven’t used your concessional contributions caps and you have under half a million in super, you can each use the carry forwards to offset the CGT,” Marinis says.
After-tax contributions People often forget about the generous rules for contributions made with after-tax money, such as paid wages or cash in the bank. These are called non-concessional contributions and their current cap is $130,000 a year, indexed in line with wages.
People can also bring forward two future years of non-concessional contributions, enabling them to pump in $390,000 in a single financial year.
It’s great for building a big balance quickly ahead of starting a tax-free account-based pension after age 60. The current starting cap for these pensions is $2.1m, known as the transfer balance cap, and it’s indexed to inflation. Given the average super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is $413,700 for men and $327,400 for women, most people have wiggle room.
Spouse contributions Want a $540 annual tax offset while boosting your better half’s super balance? You can get this by injecting $3000 a year into their superannuation fund, but your spouse must earn less than $37,000 a year to qualify. Advisers say spouse contributions are not used as much as they can be. It’s a similar story with government co-contribution, where a person who puts $1000 of after-tax money into their super this year can get $500 added by the government if they earn below $49,293.
Spouse splitting Rising Tide senior financial planner Rebecca Pritchard says shifting contributions between partners helps each make full use of their transfer balance cap. People can move 85 per cent of their super contributions to their spouse by requesting the split after the end of a financial year.
“A financial no-brainer, it uses what the household already has to balance the scales and pay less tax,” Pritchard says. “Too many couples spend years trying to minimise tax while doing nothing about the fact one spouse is heading towards retirement with significantly less super and therefore less financial freedom.” Downsizer contributions There’s another way to pump big bucks from the proceeds of non-super asset sales into superannuation quickly, but you’ll have to sell your home to access it.
“If you’re over 55 and have owned your home for more than 10 years, selling it allows a $300,000 non-concessional contribution into super, separate from the standard caps,” Pritchard says. “That’s $300,000 each within a couple.” Despite super’s allure since the Chalmers budget, don’t blindly pump every spare cent into super, experts say. Pritchard and Marinis are fans of investment bonds/insurance bonds, which are taxed at 30 per cent for 10 years but then offer tax-free withdrawals after that. Holding some shares and property outside super gives people financial flexibility. Atencia says she expects super to remain a highly effective structure for investing, although rule changes will always be part of the equation.
